Xu sued, rejected a $20k settlement, and lost, with the court ordering both sides to pay their own costs. This is a classic 'Smart Selfish' maneuver where litigation is used to enforce a minor grievance, resulting in mutual destruction of neighborly relations and financial loss. The media framing ('crushing blow') extracts attention from the tragedy of the breakdown.

- Actual Will (Real): -0.9 (Counteractive/Regressive: Mutual destruction).

Verdict: FAIL — Awakening into Destruction.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 15.0, z: 4)
The dispute involved a 3cm encroachment by a carport, leading to a Supreme Court battle that cost both parties their peace and significant money.

The Bright Side:
The court's decision to make both sides pay their own costs prevents the 'winner-takes-all' outcome that often fuels further resentment.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The error is in the Plane of Logic (Q5). The actor confused a minor physical encroachment (3cm) with a moral imperative, leading to a disproportionate response.

Social Physics Analysis:
Xu engaged in a 'Smart Selfish' maneuver, using the court to force compliance. The media outlet frames this as a 'crushing blow' to the woman, extracting attention from the neighbors' misery.

The Trajectory: The Path of Awakening into Destruction.
When you map the gap between the stated goal of 'justice' and the actual result of mutual destruction, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil.

The Unavoidable Truth: A 3cm encroachment is not worth the destruction of a neighborly relationship.

The Unavoidable Lie: The legal system can restore the peace that was lost in the courtroom.

Alethekanon:
Litigation is a blunt instrument for neighborly disputes. When pride replaces perspective, the court becomes a graveyard for community.

Awwthekanon:
It is heartbreaking to see neighbors stop speaking over a few centimeters of land. The true loss here isn't the property, but the peace that once existed between them.

Brothekanon:
Imagine spending thousands in legal fees over 3cm. That's not winning; that's just burning money to prove a point that nobody cares about.

Spirithekanon:
"Better is a dry morsel with quietness, than a house full of feasting with strife." Proverbs 17:1 — PASS (Spiritual Vector)
True wealth is found in the peace of one's home, not in the victory of a bitter legal battle.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Judge's crushing blow to woman who dragged neighbours to the Supreme Court over 3cm of land and rejected a $20k peace offering - and they don't want to speak to her anymore

A nurse from Sydney's Lower North Shore took her neighbours to the NSW Supreme Court after discovering their carport encroached by three centimetres onto her land.

Actual Article Body:
By MAISY RAE - NEWS REPORTER

Published:  20:39 AEDT, 27 October 2026   |  Updated:  20:39 AEDT, 27 October 2026

A Sydney woman who took her neighbours to the Supreme Court over a carport encroaching just three centimetres onto her property has walked away empty-handed after rejecting a $20,000 offer to settle the bitter dispute.

Jian Min Xu, a nurse from Sydney's affluent Lower North Shore, demanded $56,649 from her neighbours after a years-long battle over a tiny strip of land escalated into an extraordinary legal showdown.

But a Supreme Court judge has found her neighbours had not acted unreasonably, that their encroachments were relatively minor and that Ms Xu is not entitled to recover her legal costs.

And while the battle over the property boundary is finally over, the neighbours are understood to no longer be on speaking terms after racking up huge legal bills.

The dispute began in June 2022 when Ms Xu hired a surveyor to establish the boundary between her property and that of her neighbours, Royalston and Meredith Martin, ahead of building a new dividing fence.

The garage and carport were approximately 42 years old and had been in place for decades before the dispute erupted.

The survey revealed the Martins' carport, along with the eave and gutter of their garage, extended about 13 centimetres above her land.

A carport post also crossed the boundary by just three centimetres.

Jian Min Xu from Sydney took her neighbours to the NSW Supreme Court after discovering their carport encroached by three centimetres onto her land

A survey found the carport post encroached onto her property by about three centimetres

Ms Xu raised the issue with her neighbours in September 2023 and asked for the offending structures to be removed.

However, almost two years later, the work had not been completed, with conflicting surveys and a tradie taking out the wrong carport post, contributing to the delay.

Frustrated by the perceived lack of action, Ms Xu launched legal proceedings in July 2025 and asked for a court to order the removal of the remaining encroachments.

She also sought damages, including aggravated damages, and court orders relating to alleged trespass and interference with her land.

A further survey commissioned by Ms Xu identified additional encroachments of between one and three centimetres.

Rather than fight over the conflicting survey findings, the Martins agreed to remove the structures.

By May 2026, every identified encroachment had been removed. But the legal battle was far from over.

The following month, Ms Xu demanded $56,649.37 to settle her claim.

NSW Supreme Court Justice Ian Pike found there was no evidence of unreasonable conduct from her neighbours - Royalston and Meredith Martin

Her neighbours refused, instead offering her $20,000 to bring the proceedings to an end.

Ms Xu rejected the offer.

In a judgment handed down last week, Justice Ian Pike ordered both sides to pay their own legal costs after finding there was no evidence the Martins had acted unreasonably.

'The alleged encroachments relate to structures which have been in place since 1984,' he said.

'The boundary determination found that there were some encroachments, although it must be observed that they were of a relevantly minor nature.'

The judge found the structures had not seriously affected Ms Xu's ability to use or enjoy her property, although they could have interfered with her plans to build a dividing fence.

He also rejected suggestions her neighbours had deliberately dragged their feet over removing the structures.

'At no stage did the defendants indicate that they would not remove the encroachments. I do not regard the time taken as indicating any implicit refusal to do the work,' he said.

Justice Pike acknowledged Ms Xu's frustration over the delays but found there was no basis for concluding the Martins had abandoned their commitment to remove the encroachments.

Ms Xu told the Daily Mail last week she was disappointed by the decision and was considering an appeal.

The Daily Mail has contacted Royalston and Meredith Martin for comment.
